clue.text: Rising indications that one is frightened

definitions.text: Rising indications that one is frightened

parts.note: surface reading: signs that something is mounting, such as a growing fear
setter's reading: small bumps that literally rise on the skin when one is scared

explanation.surface: Someone's mounting signs of fear give them away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' sounds like increasing, but it is meant physically: little bumps rise up on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised pimples on the skin, caused by cold or fear, are a classic bodily sign of fright.

clue.text: A golfer upset about pro's first game

indicators.note: about means going around, so the rearranged letters wrap around the other piece
something upset is knocked out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of pro

explanation.surface: A golfer gets angry over a professional's opening game.
explanation.definitionFit: Children's pastime in which players vault over each other's bent backs, so it is a kind of game.

clue.text: Fed up, having to stop on guard

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards, backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round
to end is to stop

explanation.surface: Someone sick of it all has to quit being on sentry duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed up' reads as one phrase meaning bored; split, it is a word and its reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To protect something from attack is both to guard it and to keep it safe, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: A marginal advantage

parts.note: surface reading: a slight lead over a rival
setter's reading: something found at the margin, the border of a thing

explanation.walkthrough: The word for a narrow lead is also the word for the margin of something, so 'marginal' works twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a slight superiority over a competitor is called having this, which is also the boundary line of a surface.

clue.text: He has his own ideas on hoarding

definitions.text: He has his own ideas on hoarding

parts.words: He has his own ideas on hoarding
parts.note: surface reading: a person with strong views about stockpiling goods
setter's reading: a hoarding is a large outdoor billboard displaying promotional messages

explanation.surface: A stubborn person holds personal opinions on stockpiling.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a hoarding is a billboard, not the act of stockpiling, so the ideas are promotional slogans.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone promoting products puts their messages up on billboards, which British speakers call hoardings.

clue.text: Chips are heavenly served like this

indicators.note: the letters are dished up in a different form, like food arranged afresh on a plate

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A diner declares their fries simply divine when presented this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Seraphs are angels of the highest order, so this adjective describes something angelic or celestial.

clue.text: A loose nickname for the BBC

parts.note: taken as written
to loose a knot is to undo or untie it

explanation.surface: Someone coins a casual nickname for Britain's state broadcaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose' looks like an adjective describing the nickname, but it is the verb meaning set free.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Broadcasting Corporation is affectionately known as Auntie, for its supposedly prim, motherly manner.

clue.text: Knocks over box

indicators.note: knocked over, the word is tipped onto its head and read backwards

parts.note: raps are sharp knocks

explanation.surface: Something topples a crate.
explanation.definitionFit: Boxers practise by trading light punches with a partner, so the verbs share the sense of fighting with fists.

clue.text: Such a discussion gives opportunity for falling out

definitions.text: Such a discussion gives opportunity for falling out

parts.note: surface reading: a debate that might lead to a quarrel
setter's reading: something with no closed end lets things drop out of it

explanation.surface: A heated talk risks ending in a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falling out' suggests an argument, but read literally it is things dropping through an unclosed end.
explanation.definitionFit: A discussion without a fixed limit or conclusion is described with this term, like a container lacking a closed end.

clue.text: Provide some point to a joke

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass
a quip is a witty remark or joke

explanation.surface: Someone tries to give a joke some purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' sounds like a punchline but means a compass point, one of the four letters N, E, S and W.
explanation.definitionFit: To furnish somebody with necessary supplies or tools is to provide for them, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Wrongly presume it's the highest

indicators.note: done wrongly, the letters end up in an incorrect order that must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning not to assume falsely that something ranks top.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ranking above all others in authority or quality is greatest, top or paramount.

clue.text: Retired Thespian appearing as Shylock?

parts.note: ex means former, as one retired
a thespian is a stage performer

explanation.surface: A former stage actor takes the role of Shylock.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene suggests a theatre casting; in fact Shylock, in The Merchant of Venice, demands his pound of flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock insists on payment of his bond, making him one who demands what is owed; the question mark flags an example.

clue.text: Fed up with being drilled

definitions.meaning: second meaning: pierced with a hole by a turning tool

explanation.surface: A soldier is sick of endless parade-ground practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drilled' suggests military exercise, which fits the boredom, but it means having a hole made.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for being weary through dullness and the past participle of making a hole.

clue.text: Lacking a game to play — or rivals

definitions.text: Lacking a game to play — or rivals

parts.note: surface reading: having no fixture, as in a team without a match
setter's reading: having no equal anywhere, unrivalled

explanation.surface: A team finds itself with no fixture and no opponents.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the answer means without a game; its usual sense is having no equal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being without equal means nobody can compete, and literally the word means without a contest.

clue.text: Use fingers to eat a plum in the break

indicators.note: broken apart, the words are smashed up and their letters reassembled

parts.note: taken as written along with the following in, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone eats a plum with their hands during an interval.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'eat a plum in', with 'in' doing double duty as the start of the signal phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To handle or work something skilfully with the hands is the root sense, from Latin manus, hand.

clue.text: North-east port — part is to come down

parts.note: to sunder is to split or part
an aircraft lands when it comes down

explanation.surface: Part of a north-east harbour is set to collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' looks like a noun, a section of the port, but it is the verb to separate.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunderland is a city and harbour on the River Wear in north-east England.

clue.text: In which readers may find explosive articles?

definitions.text: In which readers may find explosive articles?

parts.note: surface reading: sensational, scandalous pieces of journalism
setter's reading: a magazine is also a store for ammunition, where explosive items are kept

explanation.surface: Readers turn to a newspaper supplement for its sensational stories.
explanation.walkthrough: A magazine is both a periodical and an arsenal store, so its articles may literally explode.
explanation.definitionFit: The supplement part of a newspaper carries features, and a weapons store holds munitions, giving two kinds of article.

clue.text: Count as an old gasbag

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Count Ferdinand von ..., the German nobleman behind the rigid airship
second meaning: an early airship, a huge envelope filled with gas

explanation.surface: An elderly windbag is reckoned a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gasbag' suggests a talkative old person; here it is a literal bag of gas that flies.
explanation.definitionFit: The German nobleman gave his title name to the rigid airships he built, which were held up by gas cells.

clue.text: Status symbols?

parts.note: surface reading: luxury goods flaunted to show wealth
setter's reading: badges or emblems that literally mark rank or office

explanation.walkthrough: A status symbol is usually a flashy possession; read literally, it is an emblem showing someone's rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Badges of office or military rank are emblems that show a person's standing, hence literal markers of status.

clue.text: It is rough, could be smoother

definitions.text: It is rough, could be smoother

parts.words: It is rough, could be smoother
parts.note: surface reading: something coarse that ought to be improved
setter's reading: it could act as a smoother, a tool that makes surfaces smooth

explanation.surface: A critic says a draft is rough and needs polishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoother' looks like a comparative adjective but is a noun: something that smooths.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrasive paper has a gritty face and is rubbed over wood to make it even, so it is a coarse smoothing tool.

clue.text: Agent upset over point in dispute

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places one piece above, and so before, the next
upset means thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
E, east, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A spy gets angry about the issue under argument.
explanation.definitionFit: To deny the truth of a claim is to contest or contradict it, so the two verbs overlap.

clue.text: Expedition has only half a tent

indicators.note: only half means the word is cut in two and its back portion dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut down

explanation.surface: A camping trip turns out to have just part of its shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' suggests a trek, but its older sense is promptness, as in 'with all expedition'.
explanation.definitionFit: Expedition can mean speed or promptness in doing something, which is the sense of hurry here.

clue.text: Order still from a photographer?

parts.note: surface reading: buy a single print from a cameraman
setter's reading: a command to keep motionless, as called out before the shutter clicks

explanation.surface: Someone buys a print from a photographer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' and 'still' read as buying a photo; really they mean a command to stay still.
explanation.definitionFit: A photographer calls out this command so the subject freezes, an instruction to stop moving.

clue.text: Major transaction sarcastically acclaimed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an important business agreement

definitions.note: the answer is an exclamation, not a past participle
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the ironic exclamation used to dismiss something as unimpressive

explanation.surface: A huge business agreement is greeted with mocking applause.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally names an important agreement, and as a scornful retort it mocks something as trivial.

clue.text: Barrel and stock of gun

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a large cask for wine or beer
second meaning: the thick end of a rifle held against the shoulder

explanation.surface: Two parts of a firearm are named.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barrel' and 'stock' look like two parts of one gun; 'Barrel' is the cask instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a large cask for liquor and the wooden rear end of a rifle.

clue.text: Criminal gets Gill confused with ale

indicators.note: confused means muddled up, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker muddles a small measure with beer and breaks the law.
explanation.walkthrough: A gill is an old British measure of liquid, a quarter of a pint, which suits the pub picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forbidden by law is unlawful, which is what the adjective criminal describes.

clue.text: American business contract with a Peruvian

parts.note: the shortened form of incorporated, placed after the names of US companies
taken as written

explanation.surface: A US firm signs a contract with someone from Peru.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a business document, but it means shorten: the abbreviation used by American companies.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca people ruled an empire centred on Cuzco in what is now Peru, so one is a Peruvian.

clue.text: All the composer required

parts.note: surface reading: everything a composer needed
setter's reading: the Italian direction in a score telling the whole ensemble to play together

explanation.surface: A composer had everything they needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All' looks like 'everything'; in a score it is the instruction for every performer to play.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian marking in a musical score means all, telling the full orchestra or choir to perform together.

clue.text: He plans the moves; I can act it out

indicators.note: acted out, the letters are performed in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A strategist boasts that they can perform the scheme themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A strategist, in chess or warfare, works out the manoeuvres in advance to gain an advantage.
